hero.name: Farhan
hero.who: a 27-year-old junior accountant in Hyderabad who keeps drifting into his inbox and videos

story.h: Busy all day, done with nothing
story.b: Farhan works at a small CA firm in Ameerpet, Hyderabad. Each morning he sits down to finish one client's bank reconciliation. He opens the spreadsheet, then his email, then the office WhatsApp group, then a cricket clip a colleague shared. Forty minutes later he is watching a food vlogger wander through the Old City, and the spreadsheet has one new row. He stays back till eight, drinking Irani chai with Osmania biscuits, and still carries the laptop home. His manager has started asking about deadlines in a polite voice that feels worse than shouting. Farhan is not lazy. He is busy from morning to night. He just cannot remember the last time he did one thing at a time.

ask.q: Farhan is busy all day but finishes little. What is the real problem?
o: His attention is spread over too many things at once
He simply needs to work longer hours to catch up
He is not suited to accounting work at all
ask.why: Farhan has the time and the skill. What he lacks is room in his mind for one task, because email, WhatsApp and videos all crowd in together. Longer hours stretch the same scattered attention, and blaming the job skips the problem he can actually fix.

chapters.take: Being busy all day is not the same as focusing on anything.

story.b: Farhan starts thinking of his attention as his small office desk. If it is covered with files, tea cups and a phone, there is no space left to work. So the next morning he closes everything except the reconciliation and the bank statement. He logs out of WhatsApp on the laptop. He skips the optional team call. For the first ten minutes it feels too quiet. Then he sinks in. Numbers start to match. He finds a duplicate entry he had missed for a week. He finishes the reconciliation in seventy minutes, a job that usually eats his whole day. He looks at the clock twice, sure it must be wrong.

ask.q: His colleague Deepa wants to join a client call while finishing tricky GST workings. What should she do?
o: Do both together, since the call is only partly relevant to her
Join on mute and check the workings during the slow parts
Finish the workings first or join the call fully, not both
ask.why: The mind can hold only a little at once. Half listening while doing careful numbers means both get done badly, and GST mistakes cost real money. Muting the call does not free the attention. Doing one task at a time gives each one full care.

chapters.take: Your attention is a small desk. Keep only one thing on it.

story.b: Some days Farhan still drifts without noticing. He opens his email to send one file and surfaces thirty minutes later, reading a thread about the office cricket tournament. So he sets a gentle reminder on his laptop for every hour. It asks one question: what should I be doing right now? He also starts each morning by writing three tasks on a yellow sticky note beside the monitor. The first time the reminder pops up, he is reading a property listing in Gachibowli he has no plan to buy. He laughs, closes it and goes back to the audit notes. By Friday the reminder has caught him three times, and each time it saves him half an hour.

ask.q: The reminder goes off and Farhan is deep in an email thread that is not his. What should he do?
o: Finish reading the thread first, since stopping halfway feels untidy
Check his sticky note and switch back to what he meant to do
Turn the reminder off, because it keeps interrupting him
ask.why: The reminder works only if he actually compares what he is doing with what he intended. Finishing the thread lets autopilot win again, and switching off the reminder removes the one thing catching his drift. A quick check pulls him back.

chapters.take: Keep asking what you meant to do, and autopilot loses its grip.

story.b: Farhan notices that most drifting starts with a ping. A WhatsApp buzz, an email banner, a cricket score alert. Fighting each one takes effort, and by noon he has none left. So he changes the setup before the work starts. Every evening he plans the next day's deep block, ten to one. In the morning his phone goes into the desk drawer, face down. Laptop notifications go off. A blocker shuts video sites until lunch. He tells the team he will reply to messages at one. The first day he reaches for the drawer four times without thinking. By the second week the drawer stays shut, and the morning block becomes the part of the day he enjoys most.

ask.q: Farhan has a heavy audit file to start tomorrow. When should he deal with distractions?
o: Tonight, by switching off alerts and deciding where his phone will go
In the moment, by resisting each ping when it arrives
After lunch, once the hardest part of the file is done
ask.why: Each ping he resists still costs a little focus, and willpower runs low when the work is hard. Waiting until after lunch means the best hours are already lost. Setting things up the night before means the temptations are simply not there when he starts.

chapters.take: Remove distractions before you begin, instead of fighting them while you work.

story.b: A new client has a messy ledger, and Farhan cannot work out how to sort it. Categories overlap, vendors repeat, and staring at the screen only makes it worse. Usually he fills his metro ride home with podcasts. This time he leaves his earphones in his bag. He just stands by the window as the train leaves Ameerpet, watching rooftops, water tanks and kites go by. His mind wanders to his mother's spice tins, then to cricket, then to nothing at all. Somewhere near Tarnaka an idea simply arrives. Sort by vendor first, then by month. He types it into his notes before the doors open. On Sunday, folding laundry, two more ideas show up the same way.

ask.q: Farhan is stuck on a problem and has a free half hour. What should he try?
o: Keep staring at the spreadsheet until the answer finally comes
Watch a few short videos to take his mind off it
Take a walk without his phone and let his mind roam
ask.why: Staring harder keeps him in focus mode, which is already stuck. Short videos fill his head with new input and leave no room for links to form. A phone-free walk gives his wandering mind space to join what he already knows, which is often when answers appear.

chapters.take: Let your mind wander on purpose. It is quietly solving things.

story.b: Farhan notices a pattern. On nights he scrolls short videos till one, the next morning feels like wading through mud, and his ideas are thin. So he makes a small swap. After dinner he reads twenty minutes of a book about how small businesses manage money. On Sundays he sits with his uncle, who runs a pharmacy in Mehdipatnam, and asks how he handles cash flow. He tries to sleep by half past eleven. Within a few weeks, something shifts at work. When a client keeps mixing up advances and payments, Farhan suggests a simple tracking sheet, borrowed from his uncle's way of doing things. His manager asks where that idea came from.

ask.q: A friend tells Farhan that reading and early nights are luxuries in audit season. What is the best reply?
o: Agree, and push the book and early nights until after the season
Explain that good input and real rest keep his focus sharp
Agree, but add an extra chai at night to stay alert
ask.why: A tired brain has less attention to give, and junk input gives a wandering mind little worth connecting. Busy season is exactly when he needs rest most, and extra chai hides tiredness without fixing it. Good books, real talks and sleep feed better work.

chapters.take: What you feed your mind, and how you rest it, shapes your best ideas.

story.b: Two months later, Farhan leaves the office before seven most days. The yellow sticky note beside his monitor still has three tasks each morning. His phone spends the mornings in the drawer, and the blocker runs till one. He still watches cricket highlights, but at home, on purpose, with his feet up. On the metro he looks out of the window more than at his phone. His manager has given him a bigger client and stopped asking about deadlines. Deepa asks him how he suddenly became so quick. Farhan opens the drawer and shows her the phone lying face down. She laughs. The next day her phone is in her drawer too.

chapters.take: Guard what fills your attention, and your work gets easier.
